doc.title: Rick Montalbano interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, August 12, 2011

title: Song requests and his mother's knowledge of standards
summary: Rowe remembers faking bridges on requests. Montalbano recalls his mother singing every standard from hit-parade books and his father loving Basie, so the standards were the music of his home.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: I can recall people coming up and requesting a song, “Flamingo” or even something that might have been on the radio at the time like “Spanish Eyes” or something.

And I remember specifically you’d look at Carmen and you might say a key. And on occasion you guys would play it but you didn’t know the bridge, and you’d make it up. And I would watch these people who had requested it, oh I’m so happy you played my song. I said this is important to learn.

Yeah. Well as you’re saying that I’m thinking about my mom. My mother, who you knew, she knew every song, I think every standard song ever written. She knew them all. She could sing the lyrics. She was not a musician, and she wasn’t a singer, but she would buy these books of lyrics, the hit parade books, I’m talking about from the 1940’s on. And she would look at the lyrics and every song that would come on the radio, anything that would play, bang, she would start singing. know, “please.” Yeah. So a lot of that was growing up and hearing that music. Another advantage if you’re going to play standards, and the kids today don’t necessarily get that in their homes, you know, in the background, you have to seek it out. We didn’t have to seek out that music, it was the music of our lives. That was what we heard. Sinatra and Ella and, you know, my father, another non-musician but he loved Count Basie’s band and all the great big bands and all that. So that’s kind of what we heard.
